intro_paragraphs: Palmetto Bay grew up as ranch country: low-slung 1950s-to-70s houses on lots that often top 15,000 square feet in Mangowood, Tanglewood Estates, and Coral Reef Estates, joined later by 1990s gated enclaves like Old Cutler Palms and waterfront pockets east of Old Cutler Road. The bones are usually good. The layouts are not. Owners here hire us to take a compartmentalized ranch down to block and rebuild it as one coherent house: kitchen opened to the family room, a real primary suite, new electrical, plumbing, and AC, impact windows all around, and finishes chosen once, correctly.

Your permit file goes to the Village of Palmetto Bay Building and Permitting Department on East Hibiscus Street, and contractors must be registered on the Village's online portal before anything gets filed. Because much of Palmetto Bay sits in or near a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, the floodplain math matters: on substantial improvements, the cost of the work is measured against the value of the structure, and that can shape the whole project. Add Miami-Dade's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone product approvals and DERM tree permits where the canopy is involved, and you want a contractor who has filed all of it before.

More than twenty years in South Florida and over 150 delivered remodels and additions have settled how PGX Builders Group works: permitted always, inspected always. In Palmetto Bay that means a fixed written scope before demolition, a supervisor on your site daily, and crews who respect a gated street in Royal Harbour Yacht Club as much as a corner lot near Coral Reef Park. From estimate to final inspection to warranty the same team stays on the job, which means one phone number and a person who actually picks it up.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel my home in Palmetto Bay?
faqs.a: Yes. Interior remodeling that touches structure, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical work requires permits from the Village of Palmetto Bay Building and Permitting Department, and your contractor must be registered on the Village's online portal before applying. Unpermitted work surfaces at appraisal or resale, and it surfaces expensively. PGX handles the filings, the plans, and every inspection as part of the job, which is why our projects close out cleanly.

faqs.q: How long does permitting take in Palmetto Bay?
faqs.a: The Village quotes about a week for its initial in-house review, which is fast by Miami-Dade standards. The real variable is outside agencies: projects that involve DERM, tree permits, or health department review of a septic system take longer, and floodplain review adds a step for homes in a flood zone. We build the permitting timeline into the written schedule so you know before demolition, not during.

faqs.q: My house is east of Old Cutler Road. Does the flood zone limit my remodel?
faqs.a: It can. Much of Palmetto Bay, especially toward the bay, sits in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, and the Village administers the substantial improvement rule: if the cost of improvements crosses the threshold relative to your structure's value, the home must be brought into flood compliance. That is not a reason to skip the remodel; it is a reason to scope it precisely. We run that math with you at the estimate stage.

faqs.q: Should I remodel my 1960s ranch or tear it down and build new?
faqs.a: Usually the ranch wins. Most of these houses are solid CBS construction with straightforward rooflines, which makes them excellent candidates for gut renovation, structural openings, and even second stories. New construction triggers today's full code and flood elevation requirements from scratch, and it costs accordingly. We will tell you honestly if your house is the exception; we have walked away from remodels that did not deserve saving.

faqs.q: What does a whole-home remodel cost in Palmetto Bay?
faqs.a: It depends on square footage, structure, and finish level, and anyone who quotes a number before walking the house is guessing. We work at the high end of the market: custom cabinetry, natural stone, engineered openings, full systems replacement. What we commit to is a fixed written scope and price before work starts, so the number you approve is the number you pay unless you change the plan.

kitchen-remodeling.local_heading: Why Palmetto Bay kitchens get rebuilt
intro_paragraphs: Walk into an original kitchen in Mangowood, Tanglewood Estates, or Coral Reef Estates and you will usually find the same thing: a closed galley from the sixties or seventies, walled off from a family room that everyone actually lives in. The remodel owners want here is not cosmetic. It is the wall coming out, a ten-foot island going in, custom cabinetry to the ceiling, natural stone with waterfall edges, and appliances relocated to where a cook would have put them in the first place.

Because those walls are often load-bearing block and those moves involve gas, electrical, and plumbing, a real Palmetto Bay kitchen remodel is a permitted project. Plans go to the Village of Palmetto Bay Building and Permitting Department, structural openings get engineered and inspected, and any contractor doing the work must be registered on the Village's permitting portal. There is no separate design review board second-guessing your kitchen; review here is about code, which suits us, because code is a thing we are extremely good at.

The high-end difference shows up in the tolerances. PGX builds kitchens around shop drawings, not catalog guesses: cabinetry scribed to out-of-level sixties slabs, stone templated after the boxes are set, lighting placed for the island you are getting rather than the room you had. A supervisor checks the site daily, the rest of your house stays sealed off and clean, and the schedule is written down before demolition. After twenty-plus years and more than 150 remodels in South Florida, we have learned which shortcuts to refuse.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel a kitchen in Palmetto Bay?
faqs.a: If the project moves plumbing, gas, electrical, or walls, yes, and most good kitchen remodels do. Permits come from the Village of Palmetto Bay Building and Permitting Department, and inspections happen at rough and final stages. A purely cosmetic swap of doors and counters may not need one, but that is rarely the project owners here actually want. We fold permitting into the schedule so it costs you no attention.

faqs.q: Can you remove the wall between my kitchen and family room?
faqs.a: Almost always. In Palmetto Bay's CBS ranches that wall is frequently load-bearing, which means an engineer sizes a beam, the Village reviews the plans, and the opening is built and inspected properly. It is a routine move for us and the single highest-impact change most sixties and seventies floor plans can make. The house feels a decade newer before the first cabinet arrives.

faqs.q: Can we live in the house during the kitchen remodel?
faqs.a: Most Palmetto Bay clients do. We seal the work zone with dust barriers, protect floors along the crew path, and help you set up a temporary kitchen, usually in the laundry room or on a covered terrace. The noisy, dusty phases are scheduled and announced in advance. It is not glamorous, but with a big lot and a written schedule it is entirely livable.

faqs.q: How long does a full kitchen remodel take?
faqs.a: Plan on several months from design approval to final inspection, with custom cabinetry lead time usually setting the pace rather than construction itself. Village permitting for a straightforward kitchen is quick; structural openings or service relocations add review time. We order long-lead items before demolition so the house is never torn open while everyone waits on boxes. The written schedule you approve shows every phase.

faqs.q: What does a high-end kitchen remodel cost in this area?
faqs.a: For the level of work Palmetto Bay owners hire us for, custom cabinetry, natural stone, engineered openings, relocated services, budgets land well into six figures, and the spread depends mostly on cabinetry and stone selections. We are not the cheap bid and do not pretend to be. What you get for that is a fixed price on a defined scope, and a kitchen that appraises as well as it photographs.

bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Primary-suite and guest bath remodeling across Palmetto Bay: frameless showers, freestanding tubs, stone done right, and waterproofing built to code. Licensed, insured, permitted through the Village, and supervised every working day.
intro_paragraphs: Nothing dates a Palmetto Bay house faster than its bathrooms. A well-kept ranch in Tanglewood Estates or Mangowood will still hide a 1970s hall bath behind its oak door: low ceiling, tub nobody uses, a vanity built for smaller mornings. Owners here are converting spare bedrooms and closets into genuine primary suites, with curbless showers behind frameless glass, freestanding tubs, book-matched stone, and double vanities under proper lighting. Done well, it is the room that changes how the whole house feels at 6 a.m.

Bathroom work in Palmetto Bay is permitted through the Village's Building and Permitting Department, with plumbing and electrical inspected at rough and final. Two local wrinkles matter. First, many original homes still drain through decades-old cast iron under the slab, and a remodel is the sensible moment to camera and replace it. Second, a fair number of properties here run on septic systems, so adding fixtures or moving a bathroom can bring Miami-Dade County review of the system's capacity. Neither is a crisis. Both are things to know before tile is ordered.

Waterproofing is where we are frankly obsessive. Every PGX shower gets a full membrane system, flood-tested before a single tile goes on, because stone and glass are only as good as what is behind them. The scope is fixed in writing, a supervisor walks the site daily, and floors between the front door and the bath are protected for the duration. One team runs demolition through final inspection and warranty. It is the least dramatic way to build a bathroom, which is exactly the point.

faqs.q: Do bathroom remodels in Palmetto Bay require permits?
faqs.a: Yes, once you touch plumbing, electrical, or walls, which describes any remodel worth doing. The Village of Palmetto Bay issues the permits and inspects the work at rough and final stages, and contractors must be registered with the Village before filing. It is a straightforward process when your plans are complete and your contractor is organized. Ours are; that is most of the trick.

faqs.q: My home is on septic. Can I still add a bathroom?
faqs.a: Usually yes, and it is a common question in Palmetto Bay because many neighborhoods here predate sewer connections. Adding fixtures or bedrooms can trigger a county-level look at your septic system's capacity, and occasionally a drainfield upgrade. We flag this at the estimate stage, before design money is spent, so the answer arrives early instead of mid-project. If your street has sewer available, we can talk through connection as part of the work.

faqs.q: How long does a primary bathroom remodel take?
faqs.a: Typically two to three months of construction once permits are in hand, plus lead time for glass, stone, and plumbing fixtures. Flood-testing the waterproofing adds a day nobody should ever skip. If we discover failed cast iron under the slab, replacing it adds time and we will show you the camera footage rather than ask you to take our word for it.

faqs.q: Can you turn two small bathrooms into one large primary bath?
faqs.a: That is one of our favorite Palmetto Bay conversions. Ranch-era plans often placed two modest baths back to back, sharing a wet wall, which makes combining them efficient: plumbing stays close, and the result is a genuinely large suite bath instead of two apologies. It requires a permit, some re-framing, and occasionally structural work, all of which is normal scope for us.

faqs.q: What should I budget for a high-end bathroom remodel?
faqs.a: Less than a kitchen, more than the tile-store math suggests. Stone, frameless glass, fixtures, and proper waterproofing carry real costs, and moving plumbing adds more. We serve the upper end of the Palmetto Bay market and price accordingly: a fixed written number for a defined scope, no allowance games, no surprise change orders for things we should have seen. We would rather lose a bid than pad one.

home-additions.local_heading: Room to grow in Palmetto Bay
intro_paragraphs: Palmetto Bay families tend to stay put, and it is easy to see why: big lots, good schools, canopy streets, and Coral Reef Park down the road. So instead of leaving, owners in Tanglewood Estates, Coral Reef Estates, and East Palmetto Bay extend. The classic moves are a rear family-room wing opening to the yard, a primary-suite addition, a garage converted into an in-law suite, or a full second story on a one-level sixties ranch. On lots this size, the architecture has room to breathe while the addition earns its keep.

Additions here answer to the Village of Palmetto Bay Building and Permitting Department, and to a few realities beyond it. Zoning setbacks and lot coverage limits shape the footprint. The Village administers FEMA floodplain rules, so on homes in a Special Flood Hazard Area, particularly east of Old Cutler Road, the substantial improvement calculation can influence how much you build at once. Palmetto Bay is also a Tree City USA community, and removing or building near protected trees means a Miami-Dade DERM permit. None of this is a problem for a contractor who plans for it on day one.

An addition lives or dies at the connection points, which is why PGX starts with structure: foundations tied correctly to the existing slab, tie beams and columns engineered for wind load, and a roof line that reads as original rather than annexed. You get a fixed written scope before ground breaks, a supervisor on site daily, and stucco and finishes matched so closely the addition disappears. With more than 150 remodels and additions behind us in South Florida, we know exactly where these projects go wrong, and we schedule those spots first.

faqs.q: Can I add a second story to my Palmetto Bay ranch?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many of the village's CBS ranches can carry a second floor once an engineer verifies the foundation and we add the required columns and tie beams. Where the existing structure will not cooperate, a partial second story or a rear wing usually gets you the space anyway. We give you a structural read early, before you fall in love with a drawing the house cannot support.

faqs.q: How close to my property line can I build an addition?
faqs.a: It depends on your zoning district, and Palmetto Bay's setbacks and lot coverage rules are specific enough that guessing is a bad idea. Part of our pre-design work is confirming exactly what your lot allows with the Village, including any corner-lot or easement quirks, before the architect draws a line. On the large lots common here, the honest answer is that setbacks rarely kill the project; they just shape it.

faqs.q: Does the flood zone affect my addition east of Old Cutler Road?
faqs.a: It can, and it is worth checking before design starts. The Village administers FEMA floodplain rules, and for homes in a Special Flood Hazard Area the substantial improvement calculation compares your project cost to the structure's value. Cross the threshold and flood compliance obligations follow. Sometimes the smart answer is phasing the work; sometimes it is building the addition at the required elevation from the start. We map this out with you before permitting.

faqs.q: Will you have to remove trees for the addition?
faqs.a: We try hard not to, and Palmetto Bay would prefer we did not either. The village takes its canopy seriously, and protected trees require a Miami-Dade DERM permit to remove or relocate, sometimes with mitigation planting. Good siting usually solves it: we shift the footprint, adjust the foundation approach near root zones, and save both the oak and the argument. When removal is unavoidable, we handle the permitting rather than hoping nobody notices.

faqs.q: How long does a home addition take from design to done?
faqs.a: Plan in seasons, not weeks. Design and engineering come first, then Village review plus any county-level sign-offs, then construction, which typically runs several months depending on size and structure. A second story takes longer than a rear wing. What we control tightly is the construction schedule itself: materials ordered before demolition, inspections booked ahead, and a written timeline you can hold us to.

outdoor-living.local_heading: Outdoor living in the Village of Parks
intro_paragraphs: In Palmetto Bay, the lot is half the reason you bought the house. This is the self-declared Village of Parks, with Coral Reef Park up the road and the Deering Estate anchoring Old Cutler Road, and yards here run large enough for real outdoor rooms rather than a token patio. Owners across Mangowood, Coral Reef Estates, and East Palmetto Bay hire us for covered terraces with tongue-and-groove ceilings, summer kitchens that can actually host, pergolas over dining areas, and driveways and entries upgraded to match the house behind them.

Outdoor structures in Palmetto Bay are permitted work: anything with footings, a roof, gas, or electrical goes through the Village's Building and Permitting Department, and in Miami-Dade's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, pergolas and covered terraces must be engineered for wind load with county-approved products, not assembled from a kit and optimism. The village's tree rules matter outdoors most of all, since driveways and slabs near protected root zones can require DERM permits and careful design. Waterfront owners east of Old Cutler Road also plan around flood zones when adding hard structures.

What PGX brings outdoors is the same discipline we bring inside: one contractor responsible for the slab, the roof tie-in, the gas line to the grill, the electrical, and the finish work, instead of four trades pointing at each other. The scope and price are fixed in writing, a supervisor is on site every working day, and lawns, pool decks, and gated entries are protected and kept clean, which your neighbors in a community like Royal Harbour Yacht Club will quietly appreciate. Twenty-plus years in South Florida taught us that outdoor work is judged in August, not on delivery day.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a pergola or covered terrace in Palmetto Bay?
faqs.a: Yes. Structures with footings or a roof are permitted through the Village of Palmetto Bay, and because all of Miami-Dade sits in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, they must be engineered for wind load using county-approved products. The unpermitted kit pergola is a familiar sight here right up until a storm or a home sale, whichever comes first. We design, permit, and build them to stay.

faqs.q: Can you build a summer kitchen with a gas line?
faqs.a: Yes, and running the gas correctly is most of the job. Whether your home has natural gas service or a propane tank, the line to a summer kitchen is permitted and inspected work, alongside the electrical for refrigeration and lighting. We coordinate all of it under one permit package with the Village, pour the slab and counters, and hand you a cooking space that works as hard as your indoor kitchen.

faqs.q: Will Palmetto Bay's tree rules affect my driveway or terrace plans?
faqs.a: Quite possibly, and better to know early. The village guards its canopy, and work near protected trees, including new driveways, slabs, and footings in root zones, can require a Miami-Dade DERM tree permit. In practice this shapes design more than it blocks it: we route hardscape around significant trees, adjust footing locations, and pull the tree permit when one is genuinely needed. The oaks were here first; the terrace can be diplomatic.

faqs.q: Can outdoor projects be combined with impact windows or a re-roof?
faqs.a: That is often the smartest sequencing. If the exterior is getting scaffolding and permits anyway, bundling stucco, paint, impact openings, and re-roof coordination with the terrace or summer kitchen saves mobilization costs and repeated disruption. It also means one contractor owns the waterproofing story where roof, wall, and new structure meet, which is exactly where leaks are born when trades work separately.

faqs.q: What does a covered terrace or outdoor kitchen cost?
faqs.a: A pergola over an existing slab and a fully roofed terrace with a summer kitchen live in very different budgets, so we scope before we quote. Engineering, permitted gas and electrical, and hurricane-rated materials are where the money goes, and they are also why the result lasts. Expect a fixed written price from us rather than a teaser number that grows, and expect us to suggest cuts if your wish list outruns the value.

permitting-compliance.local_heading: The Village kept its own building desk
intro_paragraphs: Palmetto Bay is mostly 1950s-to-70s ranch houses on big lots: Mangowood, Tanglewood Estates, Coral Reef Estates, the streets east of Old Cutler Road. Nearly all of them have passed through three or four owners, and somewhere in that history sits a carport turned into a bedroom, a patio enclosed and air conditioned, an electrical panel swapped on a Saturday. Structural, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work all require permits here, and so do roofing, windows and doors, fences, sheds, pools and standby generators. What was skipped decades ago does not disappear. It waits for an appraiser, an inspector, or a buyer.

Permits for those houses are filed with the Village of Palmetto Bay Building and Permitting Department on East Hibiscus Street, where the Building Official also administers the floodplain. Your contractor has to be registered on the Village's portal before an application can be submitted at all. County agencies still attach to a scope though the Village issues the permit: Miami-Dade's Board of Rules and Appeals oversees code administration countywide, environmental review reaches protected trees, the county health department handles septic systems, and Miami-Dade product control governs anything meant to survive a hurricane. And permits issued before the Village incorporated in 2002 live in the county's records, not the Village's.

PGX Builders Group has spent more than twenty years filing in South Florida, and every one of our 150-plus remodels and additions has been permitted and inspected. On compliance work that means we pull the record first and tell you what it says, coordinate the engineer, architect or surveyor the file needs, and put the corrective scope in writing before anyone touches the house. We do not expedite anything improperly, and we do not promise an outcome the code will not give you. What we do promise is one accountable team, a supervisor on site, and a permit that ends in a final inspection instead of a question.

faqs.q: There is an open permit on my Palmetto Bay house from a previous owner. Can I still sell?
faqs.a: You can list it, but it has to be resolved, and closing out permits commonly lands on the seller, so read what your contract actually says. Start early. The Village's lien search returns open and expired permits from both Palmetto Bay and Miami-Dade County, because the county issued the permits here until the Village incorporated in 2002. Once we see the record we can tell you whether the fix is an inspection, a reinstatement, or real corrective work. Plan on weeks, not days.

faqs.q: How long does it take to close out a permit, and can you speed it up?
faqs.a: Nobody jumps the line legitimately, and anyone who says otherwise is selling you a problem. What saves time is a complete first submittal and a scope that anticipates what the inspector will ask to see. A simple closeout moves quickly. A permit whose work has to be exposed, corrected and re-inspected does not. Weeks, not days, is the honest frame, so tell us about a closing date up front.

faqs.q: What actually needs a permit in Palmetto Bay?
faqs.a: More than owners expect. Anything structural, electrical, plumbing or mechanical, plus roofing, windows and doors, fences, sheds, pools, decks, driveways and standby generators. Interior finish work, meaning paint, flooring over an existing slab, or swapping cabinets in place, generally does not, until it moves a wall or a pipe. If the scope touches a protected tree or a septic system, county agencies review it too. When it is genuinely unclear, we ask the Village instead of guessing.

faqs.q: Do my windows and doors really need Miami-Dade approved products?
faqs.a: Yes. All of Miami-Dade sits in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone, so windows, doors, garage doors, roofing and skylights need a current product approval covering your specific size and design pressure, installed exactly the way that approval describes. The documentation gets checked at inspection. Buying glass that carries no approval, or anchoring it the wrong way, is how a job fails an inspection and stalls a schedule that had no room in it.

faqs.q: My building received a recertification or milestone inspection notice. Can PGX handle it?
faqs.a: We handle the construction side. A licensed engineer or architect performs the inspection and signs the report; we coordinate that professional, then permit and build the repairs it calls for. In Palmetto Bay this rarely touches a house, since single-family homes and duplexes sit outside Miami-Dade's recertification program. It does reach the village's older multi-family and condo buildings, and any condominium three habitable stories or more in height falls under the state's milestone and structural reserve rules. Check your building's age rather than trusting the old forty-year number.
